<meta>continues from previous page: the knowledge itself grasps that it is.</meta>

Why, then, and in what way does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if He judges that things which are avoidable will happen, and yet it is impossible for them to happen, He is mistaken; to believe such a thing is not only a sin <note>original: "nephas," meaning a violation of divine law</note> but even a sacrilege to speak. But if He discerns that future events are to be as they are, in such a way that He knows they can either happen or not happen, what kind of <term>prescientia</term> <gloss>foreknowledge</gloss> is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous <note>The OCR reads "radicalo," likely a printer's error for "ridiculo," referring to a famous line from Horace's Satires</note> prophecy of <term>Tiresias</term> <gloss>the blind seer of Thebes</gloss> who said: "Whatever I say will either happen or not"? In what way would divine <term>prudentia</term> <gloss>wisdom or providence</gloss> differ from human opinion, if He judges uncertain things whose outcome is uncertain, just as men do? But if nothing uncertain can exist in that most certain source of all things

<summary>Boethius questions how divine foreknowledge can be certain if future events are dependent on free will and remain avoidable. He compares uncertain foreknowledge to human opinion or the meaningless prophecies of Tiresias.</summary>

<keywords>divine foreknowledge, prescientia, free will, Tiresias, providence, certainty, human opinion, Boethius</keywords>
